results.title: Exoscale pricing explained
highlights:
Published by Costfluent Published 22 October 2026 9 min read

Exoscale pricing is instances per second by size and family, local SSD storage and block storage per GiB-hour, SOS object storage per GiB-hour in volume tiers, a Kubernetes control plane per hour, elastic IPs and load balancers per hour, and outbound traffic per GiB above an allowance per instance, all without tax in the account's currency, euro, francs or dollars. On the bill the instances with their local storage that run through the month dominate; traffic appears only once an instance sends more than about 1 TiB a month outward.

## Pricing dimensions

Exoscale bills every instance, storage and network resource for its exact usage time, down to the second, and without a monthly cap, while subscriptions such as DNS and the support plans run by the month; the pricing page shows hourly prices in euro, francs or dollars, the account currency is set at signup by the customer's legal residence, and every price excludes tax. The standard instances are available in every zone, Frankfurt and Munich included; the prices here are in euro.

| Dimension | Unit | What drives it | Optional |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Instances | Second per size and family | Standard: Micro (1 core, 512 MB) EUR 0.00729, Small (2 cores, 2 GB) EUR 0.02333, Medium (2 cores, 4 GB) EUR 0.04666, Large (4 cores, 8 GB) EUR 0.09333, Huge (8 cores, 32 GB) EUR 0.37334, Jumbo (24 cores, 225 GB) EUR 2.24 per hour; CPU- and memory-optimised families at another ratio; GPU families per zone | No |
| Local SSD storage | GiB per hour per instance volume | EUR 0.00014 per GiB-hour (storage-optimised family 0.00006); not in the instance price, charged while the instance is off | No, 10 GB minimum |
| Block storage | GiB per hour | EUR 0.00014 per GiB-hour for volumes and volume snapshots, 1 GiB to 10 TiB | Yes, from the Small size |
| Instance snapshots | GiB per hour by the source volume's size | A snapshot of a 100 GB instance counts 100 GB | Yes |
| SOS object storage | GiB per hour in tiers | Standard EUR 0.0000275 up to 512 TiB, EUR 0.00001875 to 1 PiB, EUR 0.00001389 beyond, cumulative; archival EUR 0.00000626 on request with a 10 TB minimum; objects at least 128 KiB | Yes |
| Outbound traffic | GiB per month above the allowance | 1.42 GiB per hour per instance free, about 1 TiB a month; beyond that EUR 0.02 per GiB; inbound, intra-zone and inter-zone free | Only above the allowance |
| Elastic IP and load balancer | Hour per address or balancer | Every instance includes one IPv4 and IPv6; further elastic IPv4 EUR 0.01389 per hour; network load balancer EUR 0.03472 (IPv4) or EUR 0.02083 (IPv6) per hour | Yes |
| SKS Kubernetes | Hour per cluster | Starter free without SLA; Pro EUR 0.054995 per hour with a 99.95 percent SLA; nodes as instances | Yes |
| Licences and support | Hour per Windows licence; month per support plan | Windows EUR 0.01111 up to 7 vCPU, EUR 0.02222 from 8; support Starter EUR 50, Pro EUR 500 per month, Enterprise 5 percent of usage | Yes |

Per-second billing without a cap is the trait of this model: an instance costs exactly its runtime, and the pricing page calculates monthly figures only as an aid. The local SSD storage is not in the instance price and keeps running while the instance is switched off, as do licences; a Small with 50 GB of local storage pays per month EUR 0.02333 times 720 hours for compute and 50 times 0.00014 times 720 for storage. The families differ in the ratio of cores to RAM, the CPU-optimised Extra-large with 8 cores and 16 GB costs EUR 0.23333 per hour; what families mean at the hyperscalers is in virtual machines and instance families.

The second-exact compute price excludes the local storage and licences, which keep running while the instance is off, and traffic bills only above the per-instance allowance

...

Usage data comes at three levels. The portal shows under Organization, Billing and Usage Details the running usage with a price estimate, refreshed hourly, aggregated by product and product type, without detail per resource. Invoices and usage reports come monthly as PDF and JSON with the amounts per product; the API returns them through GET /usage-report with a period in the format YYYY-MM, with quantities and units, not prices, and the CLI through exo x get-usage-report. Detailed reports per resource and service, as JSON and XLS per month, are included only with one of the higher support plans and land in an SOS bucket named usage-reports plus the organization's UUID. The prices themselves sit on the pricing page and in the calculator. Whoever needs cost per resource and hour therefore combines the usage report with the price list or books the support plan; what that means for FOCUS columns is in collecting cost data from European providers.

...

List prices in euro without tax, valid in every zone and so in Frankfurt too, read on 2026-10-21: a Standard Medium (2 cores, 4 GB) costs EUR 0.04666 per hour, EUR 33.60 in 720 hours, plus 50 GiB of local storage for EUR 5.04; a Standard Large (4 cores, 8 GB) EUR 0.09333 per hour, EUR 67.20 in 720 hours; an SKS Pro cluster EUR 0.054995 per hour, EUR 39.60; SOS Standard EUR 0.0000275 per GiB-hour, EUR 0.0198 per GiB in 720 hours; outbound traffic above the allowance EUR 0.02 per GiB, EUR 20.48 per further TiB; an elastic IPv4 EUR 0.01389 per hour, EUR 10.00 in 720 hours. The figures show that the local storage of a small instance adds about 15 percent to the compute price, that a Pro cluster costs more than a Medium instance, and that 1 TiB of egress per instance stays free while the second TiB costs EUR 20.48.

results.title: Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16 | GPUJournal
highlights:
# Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16

Nov 6, 2026

Read on Lambda's own pricing page today, Nov 6, 2026: the Instances table now prints the prices that take effect on Nov 16, 2026 — HGX B200 up $1.00 an hour, H100 up $0.60 and A100 80GB up $0.40. It is the largest single announced rise we have caught this autumn, and renters have ten days' notice.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on lambda.ai/pricing

What was announced, in the pricing page's own words (read Nov 6, 2026): 'These prices take effect November 16, 2026, at 00:00 UTC. Until then, log in to your Lambda Cloud account to see current pricing.' The printed Nov 16 rates: HGX B200 $7.69 an hour (from the $6.69 last verified on Nov 5, +14.9%), HGX H100 $4.59 (from $3.99, +15.0%), HGX A100 80GB $3.19 (from $2.79, +14.3%), and HGX A100 40GB unchanged at $1.99. Lambda is also now at a new address — lambda.com — announced on its blog on Nov 5, 2026; the pricing page itself still answers at lambda.ai/pricing.

How we are treating it: an announced rise is not a live price. Our board keeps Lambda's last verified rates until Nov 16 and will move only when the new rates are re-verified in effect on or after that date — the rise is recorded in Price Watch today as announced, with both dates. One consequence of the announcement is already live, though: Lambda's currently-effective rates can no longer be read on its public page, only after logging in, so today's public check could verify the future rates but not re-read the current ones.

What it does to the board when it lands: Lambda's B200 at $6.69 is currently the cheapest verified HGX B200 instance rate we list from a self-serve cloud; at $7.69 it would sit above RunPod Community's $5.98 marketplace rate and just below RunPod Secure's $7.99. Its H100 at $4.59 would remain above the board's best H100 SXM offer (TensorDock, from $2.25 at an 8-GPU minimum) but move Lambda from the middle of the H100 pack toward its top. Around-the-clock, the announced rises add about $730 a month per B200, $438 per H100 and $292 per A100 80GB on a 730-hour month.

results.title: AWS vs Azure vs GCP Cloud GPU Pricing [2026]
results.author: Sana Rahman
highlights:
Cloud GPU pricing used to be a simple spreadsheet exercise: look up the hourly rate for an H100 instance, multiply by the hours you need, pick the cheapest provider. In October 2026 that spreadsheet broke. AWS raised its Blackwell B200 Capacity Block rate by roughly 15% on October 7, Microsoft Azure is one of the only major clouds still publishing a flat per-GPU hourly rate for H100 capacity, and Google Cloud has yet to post an official list price for H100, H200 or B200 instances at all. Comparing AWS vs Azure vs GCP cloud GPU pricing now means comparing three different billing philosophies, not just three price tags.

...

AWS leans heavily on EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, a reservation product with dynamic pricing that changes with ... AWS’s own Capacity Blocks documentation confirms Capacity Blocks can reserve up to 64 instances, or as many as 512 H100 GPUs, with reservations bookable up to eight weeks in advance. That flexibility is useful for training runs with a known start date, but it also means there is no single “AWS H100 price” the way there used to be with plain on-demand EC2.

Microsoft Azure, by contrast, still publishes retail, pay-as-you-go rates for specific H100 virtual machine sizes. That transparency makes Azure the easiest provider to quote cleanly in a comparison article, which is exactly why most of the concrete numbers in this piece come from Azure’s own SKUs. Google Cloud sits at the opposite end: its A3 (H100), A3 Ultra (H200) and A4 (B200) instance families are confirmed to exist and to use those specific Nvidia GPUs, but no official Google Cloud page in the current research set states a public hourly price for any of them. Google increasingly routes customers toward Flex-start scheduling and committed-use contracts instead of a posted rate.

...

What AWS has not done, at least not in any officially confirmed source available as of October 23, 2026, is publish a flat on-demand hourly price for P5, P5e, P5en or P6-B200. Capacity Block pricing is explicitly dynamic, and AWS’s public materials direct buyers to request a quote or check the Capacity Blocks console rather than read a rate card.

...

Azure’s current GPU VM lineup for AI training includes NC40ads H100 v5, ND96isr H100 v5 and ND96isr H200 v5. Two of those SKUs give us the cleanest published numbers in this entire comparison. The NC40ads H100 v5 size, a single-H100 configuration, carried a reported East US pay-as-you-go Linux rate of $6.98 per hour as of October 19, 2026. The larger ND96isr H100 v5 size, which packs eight H100 GPUs, was reported at $98.32 per VM-hour in East US on the same date, which works out to $12.29 per GPU-hour.

Azure also lists an ND96isr H200 v5 size with eight H200 GPUs carrying 141 GB of memory each, making it the newest Hopper-class GPU family Azure has confirmed. Microsoft has not published an officially confirmed Azure B200 virtual machine family or hourly price as of October 23, 2026. Separately, Microsoft Foundry’s managed-compute tier, still in preview, bills hourly per accelerator across A100, H100, H200 and MI300 GPU families, but Microsoft’s documentation says rates vary by accelerator family, region, deployment scope and commitment term, and directs customers to the Azure Pricing Calculator rather than a published table.

...

Google Cloud confirmed on October 2, 2026 that its A3 instance family is powered by Nvidia H100 Tensor Core GPUs, while A3 Ultra instances carry Nvidia H200 Tensor Core GPUs. The newer A4 family, confirmed October 21, 2026, uses Nvidia HGX B200 GPUs, with the a4-highgpu-8g configuration packing eight B200 GPUs per instance. None of these three families has a confirmed, officially published public hourly price in the current research set. Google’s materials mention multiple consumption models for these instances, including on-demand, Spot and committed-use pricing, but do not spell out the specific rates for A3, A3 Ultra or A4.

...

## Cloud GPU Pricing Compared: What’s Published vs What’s a Black Box

This is the table that matters most for anyone trying to budget an AI training run, and it is deliberately conservative: it only includes rates that each provider has actually published, rather than third-party estimates.

| GPU | AWS (published rate) | Azure (published rate) | Google Cloud (published rate) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100, single GPU | No flat rate published; Capacity Blocks price dynamically | $6.98/hour, NC40ads H100 v5, East US, captured Oct. 19, 2026 | Not published |
| H100, 8-GPU node | No flat rate published | $98.32/hour ($12.29/GPU-hour), ND96isr H100 v5, East US, captured Oct. 19, 2026 | Not published |
| H200, 8-GPU node | No flat rate published | No flat on-demand VM rate confirmed in official sources | Not published |
| B200, per GPU-hour (Capacity Block) | $14.208/hour, effective Oct. 7, 2026, up from $12.355/hour (about a 15% increase) | Not offered / not confirmed | Not published; A4 uses Flex-start scheduling instead of a flat rate |

Independent GPU-rental trackers fill in some of the gaps, but their numbers are estimates rather than official list prices and should be read that way. GPU-pricing trackers reportedly placed AWS P5 H100 Capacity Block pricing around $5.97 per GPU-hour, effective October 7, 2026, and P5e/P5en H200 pricing between $6.87 and $7.895 per GPU-hour, effective October 7, 2026, though AWS itself does not publish those as fixed rates. Axis Intelligence’s October 22, 2026 comparison floated per-hour figures for Google Cloud H200 (A3 Ultra) and B200 (A4), but the same tracker found no confirmed on-demand price for those configurations, since they were marked as not available for direct purchase, so no official Google Cloud rate exists for either one. Treat any number below these published figures as directional until a provider confirms it on an official pricing page.

...

## The October 7 AWS B200 Price Hike, Explained

The single clearest pricing move any of the three providers made in the last three months was AWS’s. Effective October 7, 2026, AWS raised its P6-B200 Capacity Block price from $12.355 to $14.208 per accelerator-hour, an increase of approximately 15%, according to GPU-pricing trackers Axis Intelligence and Dev.to’s FastGPU column, which independently captured the same before-and-after figures. For an eight-GPU P6-B200 node, the current instance-hour rate is about $113.666, a noticeable jump in monthly spend for teams running sustained training jobs.

results.title: Neocloud vs hyperscaler GPU: what capacity costs | Casitel
highlights:
Neocloud vs hyperscaler GPU rates for the H100, H200 and B200, read on 3 November 2026, with published commitment discounts and what else changes the bill.

C Compute · H100 list rates, per GPU-hour Rates read 3 November 2026

...

Each provider's own page, read 3 November 2026. Not executed prices.

...

## What the rate cards say

All rates below are US dollars per GPU-hour, taken from each provider's own page on 3 November 2026. They are list rates. They are not what large buyers sign.

Provider H100 H200 B200 What the rate is

Lambda$3.99 Not listed$6.69 On-demand, 8-GPU instance

E2E Networks$3.99$5.29$7.99 On-demand

Nebius$4.50$5.40$8.50 On-demand, HGX

CoreWeave$6.16$6.31$8.60 On-demand, North America

AWS$5.97$6.87$14.21 Capacity Blocks, a short reservation

Google Cloud$9.80$10.71 Not read Vertex AI, managed service

Oracle$10.00$10.00$14.00 Pay as you go

Microsoft Azure$12.29 Not read Not read ND H100 v5, East US

Three of these need a note. CoreWeave and Azure price a whole 8-GPU machine by the hour: $49.24 and $98.32 for the H100. The per-GPU figures above are our own arithmetic. AWS publishes a plain on-demand rate only in its calculator, so the AWS row is its Capacity Blocks price, and for the H200 it is the p5e machine (the p5en costs $7.90). Google's row is the Vertex AI managed service, which is not the same product as a bare virtual machine.

Even so, the spread is wide. The H100 runs from $3.99 to $12.29, about three times. The B200 runs from $6.69 to $14.21, about twice. Rate cards also move. In our read on 8 October, Nebius showed $3.85 for an H100. On 3 November it showed $4.50.

...

Every provider here says a commitment lowers the rate. Few publish by how much.

C Compute · published commitment discounts Read 3 Nov 2026

E2E Networks 10% to 30%, its own figure

Sakura Internet 5% for 6 months, 10% for 12

Each provider's own pages, read 3 Nov 2026. Discounts off list rates.

- CoreWeave says it offers up to 60% off its on-demand prices for committed use. That is its own claim. The page lists no committed rate.
- Azure publishes reservation prices through its public price API. For the H100 machine in East US, the one-year price works out 36% below pay as you go and the three-year price 56% below. We divided each term price by its hours.
- Google Cloud lists Flexible Savings Plan rates on the Vertex AI page. For the H200 they are $9.64 for one year and $8.57 for three, which is 10% and 20% below $10.71.
- E2E Networks says three-month, six-month and annual commitments can earn 10% to 30%, depending on length and volume.
- Sakura Internet announced on 1 July 2026 a commitment plan for one H100 plan: 5% off for six months and 10% off for twelve.
- AWS cut P5 (H100) prices by 44% for on-demand and 45% for the three-year Instance Savings Plan from 1 June 2025. Those are cuts from its earlier prices, not discounts off today's rate.
- Nebius and Lambda name no percentage. Both point large buyers to sales.

results.title: If you re-priced an H100 SXM plan around last week’s increase, it is gone: Crusoe’s published H100 read $4.50 in our October 18, 2026 catalog and $3.90 again in our October 26, … | Bobby Clay
results.author: Bobby Clay
highlights:
If you re-priced an H100 SXM plan around last week’s increase, it is gone: Crusoe’s published H100 read $4.50 in our October 18, 2026 catalog and $3.90 again in our October 26, 2026 catalog.

Its H200 did the same, from $5.40 to $4.29 across the same two catalogs. Both match our October 11, 2026 catalog, and Crusoe again holds the lowest published H100 SXM across the nine providers we track, under Lambda’s $3.99 in the same October 26, 2026 catalog.

Ornn’s Compute Price Index (OCPI), a third-party index of traded prices rather than quoted or listed ones, rose in three of four families between October 19 and October 26, 2026. B200 reached $9.76 on October 26, 2026, up from $8.41 on October 19, 2026, while the lowest published B200 across those nine held at $6.69 in our October 26, 2026 catalog.

A published rate that moves up and back between captures is a rate to date, not a rate to anchor to.

Nine providers, every figure dated.

highlights:
### One Big Thing · Phase 3 · Compute

What happened: Nebius raised on-demand GPU prices on October 1, its second hike in about three months. Independent trackers show the same direction across the market.

Why it matters: The bear case on AI infrastructure assumed GPUs lose value fast. Rental rates are the cleanest test of that assumption, and so far the test is failing.

By the numbers:

- Nebius list price for an H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour; B300 from $7.85 to $9.50.
- The Ornn H100 index settled at $3.17 on October 23, up about 4% in a month.

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Index, November 2026: H100 to B300
highlights:
Every month we check the public on-demand prices of specialist GPU clouds to set our own: CoreGPU prices every GPU at least 25% below the market median. This is the data behind that number, as listed on November 4, 2026.

## Method

- One on-demand price per provider and GPU, taken from public pricing pages or price APIs. Prices for 8-GPU nodes are divided by eight.
- Specialist GPU clouds only for the median. Hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle) are listed separately because their prices are 2.5 to 4.5 times higher.
- Monthly cost = hourly price × 730 hours. Prices exclude taxes.

## Median prices by GPU

| GPU | Prices found | Lowest $/h | Median $/h | Median / month |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA B300 | 8 | 6.60 | 8.98 | $6,552 |
| NVIDIA B200 | 11 | 5.43 | 8.19 | $5,979 |
| NVIDIA H200 | 12 | 2.90 | 4.94 | $3,606 |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM | 16 | 1.99 | 3.72 | $2,716 |
| NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 | 9 | 1.40 | 2.19 | $1,599 |
| NVIDIA L40S | 11 | 0.73 | 1.57 | $1,146 |
| AMD MI325X | 2 | 3.80 | 4.21 | $3,071 |
| AMD MI300X | 4 | 2.59 | 3.22 | $2,351 |

The lowest prices often come from marketplaces with variable host quality or from “starting at” prices that are rarely available.

...

## Hyperscalers

On-demand prices per GPU-hour at the largest clouds remain far above specialist clouds: H100 from $6.88 (8-GPU instance divided by eight) to more than $12 depending on the provider, and B300 from $15 to $17.80. Commitments of one to three years cut those prices by 30 to 56%.

## What moved in 2026

- Prices are rising again for flagships. At least one large specialist cloud announced increases of 10 to 26% on H100, H200 and B300 from December 1.
- Clusters cost more than single instances. Multi-node offers are commonly 20 to 50% more per GPU than on-demand single servers.
- Listed is not available. Several providers list GPUs with no deployable region, or “contact sales” for every flagship.
- Fees moved to storage and idle time. Egress is mostly free; stopped-instance storage, public IPs and minimum billing periods are where extra cost appears.
